counterexample: Model of the proof itself (A,B at 0, C at 1, incidents iid U[0,1], dispatched ambulances gone for good, two-incident horizon since the lone survivor costs 0.5 either way). After incident 1 at t, dispatching from the left costs t and leaves {0,1} with future expected cost E[min(t2,1-t2)]=0.25, total t+0.25; dispatching C costs 1-t and leaves {0,0} with future expected cost E[t2]=0.5, total 1.5-t. Left is better iff t<0.625. Take t1=0.6: greedy sends C for 0.4+0.5=0.9, while sending A gives 0.6+0.25=0.85. Over the whole distribution greedy costs int_0^0.5 (t+0.25) dt + int_0.5^1 (1.5-t) dt = 0.625, whereas the threshold-0.625 policy costs 0.609375. So dispatch-closest is strictly suboptimal, contradicting 0037's 'sending the closest car is in fact globally optimal' (and the informal 'you would break even at best': the penalty for passing over C is 2t1-1, which is below the fixed expected benefit 0.25 whenever t1<0.625).
